performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet, conductor
intro: Fêtes, marked Animé et très rythmé, is the second of the Nocturnes. Muted trumpets play a procession that approaches over quick violin figures, and for a few bars the two sound together across the orchestra; at the end only a distant drum and the low strings continue.

sections.label: A · Quick violins, high flutes
sections.mNote: Triplet figures pass between the strings and winds.

sections.label: B · Procession for muted trumpets
sections.mNote: A♭ and E♭ in the bass under the march

sections.label: B′ · Brass march with fast string figures
sections.mNote: The procession theme in the brass, with quick violin figures

sections.label: A′ · first tempo returns, flutes leading
sections.mNote: The first tempo returns, with flowing winds and quick cellos.

sections.label: Coda · The procession recedes
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases leave the drum and low strings behind

cues.title: Opening violin triplets
cues.text: The violins begin with quick repeated triplets, sharply accented. High flutes hold above them. Cor anglais and clarinets then enter with a rising phrase over the string rhythm.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, Kalmus reprint, printed p. 19: opening violin triplets and held flutes, then cor anglais and clarinets. https://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/variations/score/BFJ7336
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy’s programme: the procession
cues.text: Debussy’s programme placed a fantastic procession within the festivities. It approaches, passes through the crowd and merges with the dance. The orchestra keeps the marching band and the dancers going at the same time.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s introductory programme for Nocturnes, reproduced by the Los Angeles Philharmonic: https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes

cues.title: Procession, muted trumpets
cues.text: A♭ and E♭ repeat in the bass, with very soft timpani and harp. The metre changes to 2/4. Over this accompaniment, muted trumpets play the broad tune of the procession.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 10, printed pp. 43–44: Modéré mais toujours très rythmé, 2/4, A♭–E♭ accompaniment and muted trumpets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Procession theme with full orchestra
cues.text: The trumpet tune is now played with trombones beneath it. Around this march the violins play fast figures and the woodwind short bursts, and snare drum and cymbals join in. Debussy marks the brass to play with a full, ringing tone without harshness.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 13, printed p. 48: combined brass melody and quick strings, woodwind figures, snare drum and cymbals; the brass instruction asks for a ringing tone without harshness.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the first tempo
cues.text: The first tempo returns in 6/8. Flutes run above short reed phrases and repeated cello notes. The heavy brass rests.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 14, printed p. 53: 1er tempo, 6/8, flute and reed phrases, repeated cello notes, then rests in the brass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1900
cues.text: At the first performance in Paris on 9 December 1900, Camille Chevillard conducted only Nuages and Fêtes. Sirènes, with its wordless women’s chorus, was added at the complete première the following October.
cues.evidence: Premières on 9 December 1900 and 27 October 1901, conducted by Chevillard: https://imslp.org/wiki/Nocturnes_(Debussy,_Claude). The scoring and chronology are also given at https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes.

cues.title: Closing bars, snare drum and low strings
cues.text: The wind players finish their last fragments. A snare drum continues ppp, with cellos and basses playing at the tip of the bow. Debussy marks the low strings pp et toujours en s’éloignant davantage.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, printed p. 70: snare drum ppp, cellos and basses du bout de l’archet, pp et toujours en s’éloignant davantage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A♭ and E♭ begin the march
transitions.how: The tempo changes to Modéré mais toujours très rythmé (moderate, still strongly rhythmic). The dance texture thins to harp, timpani and pizzicato basses, playing softly and repeating A♭ and E♭ in 2/4. The cellos join this ostinato, and then muted trumpets play the procession’s tune above it.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 10, printed pp. 43–44. https://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/variations/score/BFJ7336

transitions.title: Dance figures return over the march
transitions.to: B′ · Brass march with fast string figures
transitions.how: The marching bass continues as trumpets and trombones broaden the tune. Above them, quick violin figures and woodwind triplets bring back the dance. Snare drum and cymbals join the crescendo. The brass are marked to play with a full, ringing tone without harshness.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 13, printed p. 48: broad brass tune against fast strings and winds, with percussion.

transitions.title: The flutes take over
transitions.from: B′ · Brass march with fast string figures
transitions.to: A′ · first tempo returns, flutes leading
transitions.how: At rehearsal 14, marked 1er tempo, the metre changes from the procession’s 2/4 to 6/8. The brass and percussion stop after the first chord. The flutes play a running line above short reed figures, and the cellos play repeated notes in the bass.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 14, printed p. 53: first tempo, 6/8 and the handover to winds and cellos.

transitions.title: The procession moves away
transitions.from: A′ · first tempo returns, flutes leading
transitions.how: The late dance breaks up into short wind phrases, each followed by a quieter brass phrase. Low-string figures continue as the other players stop. In the final bars the snare drum returns at ppp, with cellos and basses playing lightly at the tip of the bow.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, closing pages, especially printed pp. 69–70. The established coda boundary locates the retreat as a whole.

source.title: Debussy, Nocturnes, original orchestral score, Kalmus reprint of Fromont
source.locator: Fêtes, printed pp. 19–70: quick violins and held flutes at the opening, the procession at rehearsal 10, its meeting with the dance at rehearsal 13, and the final snare-drum and low-string phrases.

timeline.note: The violins run in quick groups of three beneath high, held flute notes.
Reeds play upward figures across the string figures; horns and trumpets add short calls.
Upper winds trade quick figures above moving strings and held horn notes.
Winds and strings exchange short phrases, with timpani marking the bass notes underneath.
Harps, timpani and low strings begin the procession, playing a quiet repeated rhythm.
Muted trumpets play the procession tune above the repeated low notes.
Woodwind replies and horns join the procession as the strings begin to move more quickly.
The brass procession joins the strings’ dance music, with high wind calls, both harps and percussion.
Flutes and oboes take up the quick dance again above the cellos’ pulse; the brass stops.
Piccolo and flutes play above the moving strings, with horns and timpani underneath.
Soft brass plays the procession theme while the low strings continue its repeated steps.
Brief woodwind phrases pass above soft low brass and plucked string chords.
Snare drum, cellos and basses continue quietly, the strings playing at the tips of their bows.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original orchestral work; exact performing edition unestablished
fields.note: The sources identify the work and movement, but not the parts or revision used in October 1951. The original Fromont/Kalmus and 1930 Jobert full scores were viewed. Musical annotations use shared principal passages; no claim that Ansermet follows every detail of the revised edition, no cut/repeat-order certification, and no bar-accurate score alignment. Orchestra states are explicitly provisional passage estimates, not audio instrument detection.

fields.note: Debussy died in 1918; the original score was published in 1900–01. Original and 1930 score pages were consulted as historical score evidence. This assessment of the composition is separate from sound-recording rights and does not claim rights in a modern edition, scan or arrangement.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
